'''Young Suh Kim''' (12 May 1935 – 25 October 2025) was a South Korean physicist, academic, author and researcher. He was a Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Maryland]].<ref name=ooi>{{Cite web|url=https://umdphysics.umd.edu/people/faculty/emeritus/item/268-yskim.html|title=Kim, Young Suh - UMD Physics|first=Anne|last=Suplee|website=umdphysics.umd.edu}}</ref>

Kim focused his research on [[quantum mechanics]] in Einstein's relativistic world, particle theory, and optical sciences.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://academictree.org/physics/publications.php?pid=167107|title=Young Suh Kim - Publications}}</ref> He has authored several books, including ''Theory and Applications of the Poincaré Group'', ''Phase Space Picture of Quantum Mechanics'', ''Physics of the Lorentz Group'', ''New Perspectives on Einstein's E = mc2'', and ''Mathematical Devices for Optical Sciences''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.terpconnect.umd.edu/~yskim///yspapers/index.html|title=Papers and Books published by Y. S. Kim since 1961}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://paw.princeton.edu/new-books/new-perspectives-einsteins-e-mc2|title=New Perspectives on Einstein's E = mc2|date = 19 November 2018}}</ref>

He was an honored member of the International Association of Top Professionals (IAOTP).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wboc.com/story/44559937/professor-emeritus-dr-young-suh-kim-chosen-to-be-featured-in-iaotps-top-50-fearless-leaders-book|title=Professor Emeritus Dr. Young Suh Kim chosen to be featured in IAOTP's Top 50 Fearless Leaders Book|access-date=2021-11-03|archive-date=2021-11-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211103114859/https://www.wboc.com/story/44559937/professor-emeritus-dr-young-suh-kim-chosen-to-be-featured-in-iaotps-top-50-fearless-leaders-book|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Kim died on 25 October 2025, at the age of 90.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Young Suh Kim, 1935 – 2025 |url=https://www.umdphysics.umd.edu/about-us/news/department-news/yskim.html |access-date=2026-11-03 |website=Department of Physics – University of Maryland}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Kim was born on 12 May 1935 in [[Korea under Japanese rule|Korea, Empire of Japan]]. His family moved to [[Seoul]] (South Korea) in 1946. After high school graduation in Seoul, he moved to the United States in 1954 to become a freshman at the [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]] in Pittsburgh. There, Kim received his bachelor's degree in 1958. He then went to [[Princeton University]] for graduate study in physics. There, Kim received his PhD degree in 1961. He spent one additional year at Princeton as a postdoctoral fellow.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ysfine.com/home/index.html|title=Young Suh Kim homepage|website=ysfine.com}}</ref>

==Career==
Following his post-doctoral fellowship, Kim was appointed as an assistant professor of physics at the University of Maryland in 1962. At the time, he was the youngest person to become assistant professor at the university. Kim was promoted to Associate Professor and to Full Professor of Physics later. In 2007, he became an Emeritus Professor of Physics at the University of Maryland.<ref name=ooi/>

==Research==
[[File:Bohr Einstein.jpg|left|thumb]]
Kim's most significant contribution was to provide the resolution of the Bohr-Einstein issue of moving hydrogen atoms or moving bound states.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://paw.princeton.edu/new-books/new-perspectives-einsteins-e-mc2|title=New Perspectives on Einstein's E = mc2|date=November 19, 2018|website=Princeton Alumni Weekly}}</ref> Kim was not the first one to recognize the existence of this problem. [[Paul Dirac]] made his life-long efforts to construct the quantum mechanics of bound states (like the hydrogen atom) in Einstein's relativistic world.  On this problem, Dirac published four important papers in 1927, 1945, 1949, and 1963.  Kim integrated the first three of those four papers using the mathematical formalism provided by [[Eugene Wigner]]. In so doing, Kim provided the resolution to the Bohr-Einstein issue of the moving hydrogen atom, or quantum mechanics of moving bound states in Einstein's relativistic world.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://researchfeatures.com/construction-quantum-mechanics-einsteins-world-gaps-diracs-papers/|title=Construction of quantum mechanics in Einstein's world by filling in the gaps in Dirac's four papers on this subject|date=August 23, 2021}}</ref>

===Harmonic Oscillator Wave Functions for moving Bound States===
In his study regarding quantum mechanics, Kim discussed the role of harmonic oscillators in dealing with bound states. He, together with [[Marilyn E. Noz]], studied [[Murray Gell-Mann]]’s [[quark model]], and highlighted that the oscillator wave function can explain the mass spectrum of similar particles observed in high-energy experiments. While following Paul Dirac's papers, he constructed the wave function for the moving [[bound state]]. This wave function is known as the "Lorentz-covariant harmonic oscillator wave function" or "Covariant oscillator wave function."<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kim |first1=Y. S. |last2=Noz |first2=M. E. |url=https://academic.oup.com/ptp/article/60/3/801/1848622|title=Quarks, Partons and Lorentz-Deformed Hadrons |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |date=1978 |volume=60 |issue=3 |pages=801–816 |doi=10.1143/PTP.60.801 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kim |first1=Y. S. |last2=Noz |first2=M. E. |url=https://academic.oup.com/ptp/article/57/4/1373/1933565|title=Covariant Harmonic Oscillators and Excited Baryon Decays |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics |date=1977 |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=1373–1386 |doi=10.1143/PTP.57.1373 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.8.3521|title=Covariant Harmonic Oscillators and the Quark Model|first1=Y. S.|last1=Kim|first2=Marilyn E.|last2=Noz|date=November 15, 1973|journal=Physical Review D|volume=8|issue=10|pages=3521–3527|via=APS|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.8.3521|bibcode=1973PhRvD...8.3521K|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 1977, Kim and Noz published a paper in the Physical Review discussing that the covariant oscillator wave function can synthesize the quarks and the partons.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-3051-3_27|title=Special Relativity and Quantum Theory: A Collection of Papers on the Poincaré Group|first1=Y. S.|last1=Kim|first2=Marilyn E.|last2=Noz|chapter=Covariant harmonic oscillators and the parton picture|series=Fundamental Theories of Physics|editor-first1=M. E.|editor-last1=Noz|editor-first2=Y. S.|editor-last2=Kim|date=September 6, 1988|publisher=Springer Netherlands|pages=313–316|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/978-94-009-3051-3_27|isbn=9789400930513}}</ref> In 1989, Kim reinforced this result in his paper in [[Physical Review Letters]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/276568|title=INSPIRE|website=inspirehep.net}}</ref> Kim also suggested the possibility to address the Bohr-Einstein issue of moving hydrogen atom with the synthesis of quarks and partons.<ref name="auto"/>

===Einstein's Special Relativity derivable from Heisenberg's Uncertainty Brackets===
In 1962, Dirac visited University of Maryland for one week and Kim was assigned to Dirac as a personal assistant during his visit. At the time, Dirac was working on his paper on the system of two harmonic oscillators. Kim thus had direct discussion with Dirac about the topic.<ref name="auto"/> Later, Kim described how Dirac's oscillator system leads to transformations in the five-dimensional space consisting of [[three-dimensional space]] of xyz coordinates, plus two time variables. He also focused the degrees of freedom in this oscillator system, and demonstrated the space-time symmetry of Einstein's [[special relativity]] with E=mc2. He studied Heisenberg's uncertainty relations for the two-oscillator system and discussed ten generators that satisfy the closed set of commutation relations.<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=Einstein's E = mc^2 derivable from Heisenberg's Uncertainty Relations|first1=Sibel|last1=Baskal|first2=Young S.|last2=Kim|first3=Marilyn E.|last3=Noz|date=November 9, 2019|class = quant-ph|eprint=1911.03818}}</ref> His studies suggested that this set can also serve as the closed set of commutators for the ten generators for the [[Lorentz group]] applicable to three space coordinates and two time variables if it is possible to contract the second time variables to convert them into four translation generators along the three space coordinates and along the first time variable.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Poincar\'e Symmetry from Heisenberg's Uncertainty Relations|first1=Sibel|last1=Baskal|first2=Young S.|last2=Kim|first3=Marilyn E.|last3=Noz|date=March 20, 2019|journal=Symmetry|volume=11|issue=3|pages=409|doi=10.3390/sym11030409|arxiv=1903.05348|bibcode=2019Symm...11..409B|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Lorentz Group for Optical Sciences===
Kim and his co-workers made heavy investments in the Lorentz group. They noted that Dirac's two-oscillator system is directly applicable to two-photons systems in [[quantum optics]]. The two-photon [[coherent state]] or the squeezed state of light is a representation of the Lorentz group and shares the same set of mathematical formulas with the Lorentz-covariant harmonic oscillators for moving bound states. Kim and his co-workers also explained how the Lorentz group is applicable to those instruments, including the laser cavities, multilayers, and polarization optics. On this subject, they published a book entitled ''Mathematical for Optical Sciences'' in 2019.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlEvzgEACAAJ|title=Mathematical Devices for Optical Sciences|first1=SIBEL KIM BAKAL (YOUNG S. NOZ, MARILYN|last1=E.)|first2=Young S.|last2=Kim|first3=Marilyn E.|last3=Noz|date=June 12, 2019|publisher=IOP Publishing Limited|isbn=9780750319423|via=Google Books}}</ref>
